question: Over the next quarter, your team will add new workflows to the support agent. Examples include a weekly quality review of resolved refund tickets and investigations of unusual account activity. You will not choose a decomposition pattern case by case; instead, you are writing a rule set for the design document, and each new workflow gets its pattern from these rules. Which rules should the design document contain?

options.text: Give a workflow dynamic decomposition whenever it must check several aspects of a case, because multi-aspect reviews are too complex for a fixed sequence of passes.
options.reason: The guide says the opposite: predictable multi-aspect reviews are the use case for prompt chaining, not for dynamic decomposition.

options.text: Give a workflow dynamic decomposition when it is an open-ended investigation in which each finding can change which subtask should come next.
options.reason: The guide recommends dynamic adaptive decomposition, which generates subtasks from intermediate findings, for open-ended investigation tasks such as unusual account activity.

options.text: Give a workflow a fixed prompt chain whenever it calls more than two MCP tools, so that the order of tool calls stays the same and is easy to audit.
options.reason: The guide bases the choice on whether the workflow is predictable or open-ended, not on tool count; an open-ended investigation with many tools still needs dynamic decomposition.

options.text: Give a workflow a fixed prompt chain when it reviews the same known set of aspects for every case, with one focused pass per aspect.
options.reason: The guide recommends prompt chaining (fixed sequential focused passes) for predictable multi-aspect reviews, such as the weekly ticket quality review.

options.text: Give an investigation workflow a fixed prompt chain copied from its first adaptive run, so that all later cases repeat the steps that the first case needed.
options.reason: An open-ended investigation must generate subtasks from what each case reveals; freezing the steps of one case into a fixed chain ignores later cases' intermediate findings.
